λαός, ὁ, Ion.ληός , (
v.l.λαόν, which is in all Mss. in ), cj. in ; Att.λεώς, which is also used in , , while the form λαός is sts. used in Trag., and once or twice even in Com. (v. infr. ): also in Inscrr. and Pap. (v. infr.) and in late Prose, as Foed.Byz. ap. (pl.), (pl.), , etc. (both forms in pr. nn., Λεωβώτης, Λαβώτας, etc.).
in , λαός (
λαοί
) usu. means men, i.e. soldiers, both of the whole army and smaller divisions, κριτὸς ἔγρετο λ. Ἀχαιῶν; λαὸν ἀγείρειν; πολὺν ὤλεσα λαόν: pl., ἅμα τῷ γε . . ἄριστοι λ. ἕποντ' ib.; στίχες ἀσπιστάων λ.; periphr., στρατὸς λαῶν ib.; λαῶν ἔθνος; mostly including both foot and horse, as ; but sts. λαός denotes foot, as opp. horse, ; also, a land army, opp. a fleet, , , ; also, the common men, opp. their leaders, , ; but
in , λαοί, more rarely λαός, almost always means men or people; as subjects of a prince, e.g. , , al. (λαοί is sts. so used in , e.g. , ; λαοὶ ἀγροιῶται country-folk, ; work-people, ); of sailors, ; so after , ναυτικὸς λεώς seafaring folk, ; πᾶς ὁ χειρῶναξ λεώς; ὁ γεωργικὸς λεώς (lyr.): in sg., slave, τὸν Εὐρυσθέως λεών, of Heracles, ; and so perh. λεὼς αὔτοικος (Zeleia): more generally, μέροπες λαοί, i.e. mankind, (lyr.); λ. ἐγχώριοι the natives, ib. , cf. ; esp. in Egypt, of the fellahin, - (iii B. C.), (iii B. C.), etc.; civil population, opp. priests and soldiers, (Rosetta, ii B. C.), cf. (Milet., iii B. C.), al.
people assembled, as in the theatre, ὁ πολὺς λαῶν ὄχλος, cf. (both lyr.); esp. in the Ecclesia, αἱ στίχες τῶν λαῶν: hence the phrase ἀκούετε λεῴ hear O people!—the usual way of beginning proclamations at Athens, like our Oyez! , , ; τιμῶσιν οἱ πάντες λεῴ ib. ; δεῦρ' ἴτε, πάντες λεῴ; Ἀττικὸς λεώς; ὁ πολὺς λεώςthe multitude, , etc.
in , of thepeople, as opp. priests and Levites, ; in NT, of Jews, opp. Gentiles, , , al., cf. (Jewish tombstones); of Christians, opp. heathen, , al.
a people, i.e. all who are called by one name, first in , Δωριεῖ λαῷ; Λυδῶν δὲ λαὸς καὶ Φρυγῶν; ξύμπας Ἀχαιῶν λαός, cf. , etc.; ἱππόται λαοί, i.e. the Thessalians, , cf. , . (The resemblance between λαόςpeople and λᾶοςstone (cf. λᾶας) is implied in λαοὺς δὲ λίθους ποίησε Κρονίων (in the story of Niobe); and so explains the word from the legend of Deucalion, , cf. , ; but cf. .) (From λαϝ-, as shown by the pr.names Λαϝοπτόλεμος, ϝιόλαϝος ib. (Corinth): hence prob. λήϊτον.)
